text: The sun is getting brighter. Why does it brighten while it runs down? You are looking at the light on your face and a prominence is already lifting off the limb. The danger is not that ribbon. The danger is a slow climb that is already true. It is not the spots. It is not the warming of a human century. In this film, I will show you why the light rises, what the sky was like under a fainter sun and what happens as it keeps climbing. The motion is real and it is the wrong clock. A prominence is plasma held in the sun's magnetic field. It can hang, fall back or break away. In a day, it is over. Your eyes are built for that. They are not built for the change in the title. So is the sun getting brighter? Yes. Not by a ribbon you could watch from the garden, by a slow rise in the light of the whole star, about 1% brighter in every 110 million years, as it uses its hydrogen. Schroeder and Conn and Smith published that pace in 2008 in a model of the sun's long life. What if the spots were the whole story? They are not. Across a cycle of about 11 years, the total light wobbles by about a 10th of 1%. Spots darken a patch, brighter faculae make up the rest and a little more. The wobble rises, falls and comes back. It is not a climb. The warming measured on earth is a different ledger written in the air over decades. This film does not say the sun has brightened enough in your lifetime to be that warming. Across a human life, the 1% climb is far smaller than the sunspot wobble. You will not see it and you will not feel it. Now the strange question. Why would a star brighten while its fuel is running down? The fuel is hydrogen. The ash is helium. The change sits in the core where the disc you see cannot show it. Deep inside, the sun is fusing hydrogen into helium. The net of the proton-proton chain is simple enough to say aloud. Four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus. A little mass becomes energy and that energy is the light. The radiation that leaves the surface takes eight minutes to reach you. The energy was made long before that. Here is the turn. Helium is not a second sort of hydrogen. Each helium nucleus locks up more mass in fewer particles. As the core fills with ash, fewer particles remain to hold the star up against gravity. Pressure would fall unless something else rose. So the core contracts a little. It heats. Hotter hydrogen fuses faster. Faster fusion releases more energy and the star brightens. The sun brightens because it is running down. The waste in the middle leaves the fire no choice but to burn harder. That is the first payoff. The tank is not dimming as it empties. About 1% more light in every 110 million years. For as long as this remains the star you know. The spectrum drifts only a little hotter. What changes is the amount of light, not a new color on a walk. What would you see across a hundred million years? Almost nothing at first, then a sun about 1% more severe. No mystery in it, just mass, gravity and ash. We make one of these every week. Subscribing is how the next one finds you. But the sun over your street is not the sun that a young earth knew. Wind the clock back. When earth was young, this same star was fainter. Solar models put the early sun near 70% of today's light. Roughly 30% dimmer than the disk in your sky. The 1% rule is today's pace. It is not a flat rate. You can run backwards across the whole life of the star. The young sun was the dimmer one. Then the paradox arrives. A star that faint should have left the early earth frozen. The rocks say otherwise. There was liquid water. There was an ocean. How does a dimmer sun sit over a wet world? The usual repair is the air. More greenhouse gas, carbon dioxide and early methane held heat. The weaker sunlight did not supply. The faint young sun is a paradox with an answer, not a hole in the model. The sunlight was less. The atmosphere did more. How warm that early air was is still partly unknown. What would you have seen from that shore? A sun that gave less heat, a sky that may not have been this blue and a day that was not yet yours. The light was enough for water once the air had taken its share. It was not the daylight you were standing in. Until the two suns sit side by side, the daylight you trust feels finished. It is the middle of a climb. Now run today's pace forward. 1% in 110 million years. 10% takes about 10 of those steps, a bit over a billion years. Schroeder and Collins-Smith follow the rise and place a harder limit for earth near a billion years from now, when the sun is on the order of 10% brighter. More light warms the surface, warmer air holds more water. Water vapor is itself a greenhouse gas. Why the oceans would feel it is that water in the air. Past the limit, they can begin to lose water to space. The name for that threshold is a moist greenhouse. It is not next century. It is the far side of the same climb. Could a shoreline survive it? Not one that still needs an ocean, but life under this star has a very long while yet. The number matters because of its direction. The sun does not sit still and then fail all at once. It leans brighter the whole way. The disk swells only slowly through this stretch, a little larger. The thing that changes the shore is the light. The great red swelling comes later and it belongs to another film. This one stops at the brightening. The blue can last a very long time. It cannot last forever under a star that only turns one way. However bright that future disk is, you are not standing under it. You are standing in the middle of the climb. The fainter sun is behind you. The 10% sun is further off than any civilization you can picture. Overhead is the star that learned to be this bright and it is still learning. About 1% every 110 million years. A 10th of 1% up and down with the spots. A prominence when the cameras want motion. Free clocks. Only one of them answers the title. The sun is getting brighter because the helium in its core leaves the fire no choice. Earth has lived the dimmer half. The oceans are still here because the climb has not gone too far. That is timing and it is also just the physics running in ordinary daylight. What if the real question was never whether the sun is changing, but whether you arrived while the light is still gentle enough for a blue sky. The bigger question sits in that blue. How long can it last under a star that brightens while it burns? Next door, there is a planet that may already have taken that path. Next week, what happened to Venus?
